sources.title: Two processes, two purposes
sources.summary: The first sustained published argument on the government's side of the question this archive has recorded as unanswered since 28 July: whether the Commission of Inquiry and the murder prosecution can properly run together. The column separates their purposes — systemic fact-finding against individual guilt — and makes one claim that matters more than the rest, that the Commissions of Inquiry Act already contains provisions protecting witnesses from self-incrimination, and that Parliament therefore contemplated exactly this overlap. That is a columnist's reading of a statute this archive does not hold, marked single-source; if it is right, it is the answer nobody in government has given. It also brings the 2014 MV Sewol disaster into the corpus as precedent for parallel proceedings.
claims: A signed opinion column answering the defence's argument that the Commission of Inquiry and the criminal prosecution cannot run together. Its thesis is that the two serve different functions and both can and should proceed.

It distinguishes the two: the Commission is a fact-finding exercise into systemic failure — maintenance, seaworthiness, crew conduct, regulatory compliance, prevention — while the prosecution is a narrow judicial determination of individual guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

**On the point this archive has recorded as unanswered**, it argues from legislative intent: that the Commissions of Inquiry Act contains provisions protecting witnesses from self-incrimination, which "demonstrates that Parliament understood that a Commission's proceedings could potentially intersect with other legal proceedings". **[SINGLE SOURCE]** This is the first assertion in this corpus that Guyanese law already supplies a self-incrimination protection for inquiry witnesses; it is a columnist's reading and this archive holds no statutory text against which to check it.
It argues that delaying prosecution until an inquiry reports risks evidence deterioration, fading witness memory, lost documents and extended liberty for suspects.
It cites the South Korean **MV Sewol** disaster of 2014, in which 304 died, as precedent for parallel processes: arrests within days, investigations continuing for years.
It is an opinion column carrying the newspaper's standing disclaimer, not a news report, and it is the only sustained published defence of the parallel proceedings in this corpus.

sources.title: Pres. Ali names new maritime audit team
sources.summary: The state's second investigative body in the fortnight, announced 31 July and reported 1 August. A three-member Safety and Compliance Audit Team under a former MARAD Director-General, Dr Ivor English, with Col. Julius Skeete of the GDF and Capt. Joseph Lewis. Its remit is prospective — compliance standards for marine vessels generally, rather than the Barima — and, like the Commission before it, it arrives with no deadline, no budget, no terms of reference published as a document, and no undertaking to publish. It is established by presidential directive with no statutory basis stated, and nothing in the report says how it relates to the Commission of Inquiry.
claims: President Irfaan Ali announced on Friday 31 July the establishment of a **Safety and Compliance Audit Team** to review the safety and compliance standards governing marine vessels operating in Guyana. Reported 1 August.

Three members are named: **Dr Ivor English**, a former Director-General of the Maritime Administration Department, as leader; **Colonel Julius Skeete** of the Guyana Defence Force; and **Captain Joseph Lewis**, Marine Officer and Surveyor of Ships.
Ali, quoted: "I have established a Safety and Compliance Audit Team to undertake a comprehensive review of the safety and compliance standards governing marine vessels operating in Guyana."

The remit as reported: to examine compliance with maritime safety requirements and recommend strengthened oversight, improved enforcement, and higher standards for vessels, operators and regulatory systems.

[UNRESOLVED] **No reporting deadline, no budget, no terms of reference and no publication undertaking appear in the report.** It is established by presidential directive; no statutory basis is stated.
This is a body separate from the Commission of Inquiry sworn in on 30 July, and the report does not say how the two relate.

sources.title: Govt. scapegoating MV Barima crew with 'ridiculous, vindictive' murder charges – Norton
sources.summary: The first time the opposition leader has put the charging decision in these terms: that the three charged employees are being scapegoated to shield ministers. Norton calls the charges "ridiculous, vindictive, and intended to silence the workers" and moves the question up the chain — who allowed the vessel to sail, who certified it, who supervised its maintenance. Two things in it are new to this corpus: the demand that the state say which ministries owned the cargo aboard, and the allegation that pre-departure inspection procedures broke down. Both are single-source. The piece also repeats a characterisation of the DPP's statement that this archive has already recorded as the reporting outlet's wording and not a quotation of her, and it is flagged rather than carried.
claims: **Aubrey Norton**, PNCR chairman and leader of A Partnership for National Unity, speaking at APNU's weekly press conference on Friday 31 July, calls the murder charges against the captain, chief mate and goods superintendent "ridiculous, vindictive, and intended to silence the workers".

He argues the charges are premature, laid before the Commission of Inquiry could establish a cause, and states that "nothing publicly shown so far proves that these men deliberately intended to kill passengers". **These are the assertions of an opposition leader about a live prosecution and this archive adopts none of them; the three men are charged and untried.**
He redirects the accountability question upward, asking: "Who allowed a government vessel with defective systems to sail? Who certified it? Who supervised its maintenance?"

He demands public disclosure of the complete cargo manifests, weight certificates, maintenance reports, surveillance recordings and inspection certificates — and, new to this corpus, that the state identify **which ministries owned the cargo aboard**.

[SINGLE SOURCE] He alleges that normal inspection procedures broke down before departure, and that the vessel was kept in service against the advice of professional staff. Neither is corroborated here.
He repeats the demand that Ministers Juan Edghill and Deodat Indar resign to allow an impartial investigation.

[CONTESTED] The report states that the Director of Public Prosecutions "previously acknowledged the vessel had defective navigational and safety systems". **This archive has already recorded that characterisation as a reporting outlet's wording rather than a quotation of the DPP**, and it must not be cited as her admission — see the figures page.

sources.title: Expert audit team set up to review safety, compliance standards for marine vessels – Pres Ali
sources.summary: The second source on the Safety and Compliance Audit Team, published the same day as Kaieteur News and naming the same three members, which takes the appointment out of single-source territory. It carries the fuller quotation of the remit — oversight, enforcement, and "the highest practicable standards of safety and accountability" — and gives the toll as 73 dead and 30 missing from 179, which matters because it is the outlet closest to the administration carrying 73 while the government's own information service carried 72 on 30 July.
claims: Corroborates the Kaieteur News report of the same day on the Safety and Compliance Audit Team, and names the same three members: Dr Ivor English (former Director-General, MARAD), Colonel Julius Skeete (GDF) and Captain Joseph Lewis (Marine Officer and Surveyor of Ships).

Ali, quoted on the remit: the team will "examine compliance with applicable maritime safety requirements and make recommendations to strengthen oversight, improve enforcement and ensure that our vessels, operators and regulatory systems meet the highest practicable standards of safety and accountability."

Gives the toll as 73 confirmed dead and 30 still missing from 179 aboard — the figure of record on this site, from the outlet closest to the administration, two days after the government's own information service gave 72.
[UNRESOLVED] Like the Kaieteur report, it carries no deadline, no budget and no undertaking to publish the audit's findings.

sources.title: Recovery efforts scaled down as foreign divers depart; talks on salvaging MV Barima continue
sources.summary: The practical end of the recovery operation: the Prime Minister confirms diving has ceased and the French Guiana Army, Trinidad and Tobago Coast Guard and Brazilian Navy teams have left the country, with the 18-asset deployment scaled back to patrol boats and daily aerial surveillance. About thirty people were never recovered. On the wreck he restates the position this archive has recorded throughout — the government is weighing salvage against a memorial and will be guided by the families — which sits alongside, and does not confirm, the same day's report that the President has committed to attempting a lift. The piece also dates the swearing-in of the Commission to 31 July, against 30 July everywhere else including the state's own release; recorded as a reporting error.
claims: **Diving operations have ceased.** Prime Minister Mark Phillips confirms that the teams from the **French Guiana Army, the Trinidad and Tobago Coast Guard and the Brazilian Navy** have left Guyana, described as having happened "this week".
The operation is scaled down from the 18 assets previously deployed. Patrol boats remain active and aerial surveillance flights continue daily.
Figures given: **76 rescued, 73 bodies recovered, at least 30 still missing** — consistent with this archive's figures of record.

Phillips on the wreck: the government is "contemplating whether to salvage the sunken MV Barima or preserve the site as a memorial", and "those engagements with the grieving families are ongoing", to be guided by the families' wishes.

[CONTESTED] The report states the Commission of Inquiry "was sworn in on July 31". **Every other source in this corpus, including the state's own release, gives 30 July.** Recorded as a reporting error rather than a divergence in the record.
The end of diving marks the practical close of the recovery phase with about thirty people never recovered.

sources.title: Families of 3 missing MV Barima passengers want vessel salvaged, encouraged by Pres. Ali's commitment
sources.summary: The first report that the President has committed to attempting a salvage, and it moves the state's position materially: every prior statement in this corpus either left the decision with the families or had the Prime Minister saying the wreck was likely to remain where it is. Relatives of three missing Berbicians say they were told at a meeting on 29 July that a lift could take eight to ten weeks. It is single-source, reaches the archive through families' accounts of a private meeting, and no government release confirms either the commitment or the timeframe. Recorded as a development in the state's position and not as a decision, because nothing published by the state says so.
claims: **This changes the state's recorded position on the wreck.** [SINGLE SOURCE] The report states that **President Ali has committed to attempting to salvage the vessel**, and that families were told at a meeting with him on Wednesday 29 July that the process could take **eight to ten weeks**. Every prior statement in this corpus put the decision with the families or left the wreck "likely to remain there as is".

Three missing Berbicians are named by their relatives: **Raymond Sumra** of Islington, Greater New Amsterdam; **Rawle Frank** of No. 42 Village, West Coast Berbice; and **Antoine "Tony" Harcourt**, originally of Leitchfield Village, West Coast Berbice.
Puran Grant, Raymond Sumra's uncle, on what the President told them: "What he had told me [is] he [will] try his best to bring it up."
Esther Frank, Rawle Frank's mother: "I pray that things work out with what he said", and "Try the best. Anything and get help, assistance, bring up that boat."

Brenda Elizabeth Harcourt, 81, grandmother of Antoine Harcourt, asked whether she believes he is alive: "Well, I don't think so. As far as I understand, I don't think he's alive." And: "Whether dead or alive… I would like to see him. If they would bring the body home for burial, you know."

[UNRESOLVED] No government release in this corpus confirms the commitment or the eight-to-ten-week estimate. It reaches this archive through relatives' accounts of a private meeting, reported by one outlet.

sources.title: Families wants MV Barima salvaged, says Guyana's Opposition Leader
sources.author: Sherrylyn Clarke
sources.summary: CMC-credited copy datelined Georgetown, Guyana, published 31 July. Mohamed is quoted: "The families want the vessel to float, and the families told me even if it is the bones themselves, they want the bones because it will bring some closure to them." Mohamed alleges the government resists salvage because of what would be found: "the anchor is not working, the electronic systems and only one engine was working. So that is their concern, how they will look." The piece flags this with "he alleged".
claims: CMC-credited copy datelined Georgetown, Guyana, published 31 July.
Mohamed is quoted: "The families want the vessel to float, and the families told me even if it is the bones themselves, they want the bones because it will bring some closure to them."

[ALLEGATION] Mohamed alleges the government resists salvage because of what would be found: "the anchor is not working, the electronic systems and only one engine was working. So that is their concern, how they will look." The piece flags this with "he alleged".
The government "has received several local and international offers of assistance but will be guided by the wishes of the victims' families".
"More than 30 people remain missing." No body count is given at all in this version.

[CONTRADICTS ARCHIVE] The article's final line states: "The Government has not yet announced when the five-member Commission of Inquiry, unveiled by the President last weekend would be sworn in and begin its work." The Commission was in fact sworn in on Thursday 30 July, the day before publication. This is stale wire copy running a day behind the event — a datedness failure rather than a factual dispute, but a reader relying on this item alone on 31 July would be misinformed about the Commission's status.

I'm working on doing a formal request." This is the concrete 31 July movement on the salvage question. Mohamed said relatives and survivors told him President Ali stated during a State House meeting that he doubted salvaging the vessel was feasible.

[SINGLE SOURCE] Mohamed told Kiskadee Watch he has had no government response to his salvage offer — "No update, nothing at all" — and is preparing a formal written request: "I want to write and send it to them. I'm working on doing a formal request." This is the concrete 31 July movement on the salvage question.
[SINGLE SOURCE] Mohamed said relatives and survivors told him President Ali stated during a State House meeting that he doubted salvaging the vessel was feasible.

[SINGLE SOURCE] "The government circulated documents requesting relatives consent to designating the vessel a memorial site." This is the most specific 31 July claim about the memorial proposal being reduced to paperwork put before families.
Mohamed is quoted: "The government's decision to leave the MV Barima at the bottom of the Atlantic is premature and wicked."

Mohamed is quoted: "Give me the permission to float this vessel. I will recover the vessel so that the CoI can be properly conducted," and "If the government truly has nothing to hide, then there should be no objection to bringing up the MV Barima."
[ALLEGATION] Mohamed alleged the ferry was overloaded, operating on one engine, and lacked functional emergency beacons and life rafts expired since 2022. Unproven.

Prime Minister Mark Phillips is reported as indicating the vessel would likely remain submerged owing to diving difficulties.
Mohamed says he has identified unnamed international partners with the necessary equipment and expertise.

Mohamed is quoted: "Now that the commissioners have been named and sworn in, I am disappointed, as Leader of the Opposition, that I was not consulted on their appointment," and on the closed ceremony: "The government does not want us to scrutinise the co
claims: Published Friday 31 July 2026, 2:15 AM GMT-4, bylined Staff Editor.
Opposition Leader Azruddin Mohamed called on the government "to immediately release its full terms of reference" for the Commission — establishing that as of 31 July the ToR had not been published.

Mohamed is quoted: "Now that the commissioners have been named and sworn in, I am disappointed, as Leader of the Opposition, that I was not consulted on their appointment," and on the closed ceremony: "The government does not want us to scrutinise the commissioners."

[ALLEGATION] Mohamed alleges Commissioner Captain Hamada Fouda has business interests in Guyana, "including involvement with a maritime training institution at Friendship, East Bank Demerara, and the Layali restaurant at the Pegasus Hotel", that he is close to the President, and that he played a part in selecting other commissioners. Unproven.

[SINGLE SOURCE] Kiskadee Watch documents its own attempts to verify: emails to Miranda Thakur-Deen of the Atlantic Alliance Maritime and Offshore Training Institute (AAMOTI) asking whether Captain Hassan Fouda is the son of Commissioner Hamada Fouda and whether either had involvement with the MV Barima, its operators, inspections, crew training or certification — "No response has been received."

[SINGLE SOURCE] The paper contacted Suelle Findlay-Williams, head of the President's Press Unit, who ultimately said: "Regrettably, my department has not yet been furnished with the contact details. I am sorry, but I am unable to assist at this time."

[ALLEGATION] Mohamed questions a professional connection between Commissioner Nyree Dawn Alfonso and Minister of Labour Keoma Griffith, citing the website of N. D. Alfonso & Company which had identified Griffith as the firm's Guyana correspondent. "Griffith has not responded" to questions including why his photograph had been removed from the site.
Mohamed on the ministers: "They both should be sent home pending the outcome of this inquiry and make themselves fully available to answer any questions the commission may have."
Mohamed on payments: "No family should be pressured into signing any document or forced to accept any meagre sum of money."

[SINGLE SOURCE] The article sets out ToR content as reported: "the ferry's loading, passenger-boarding procedures, seaworthiness, maintenance, the competence of the crew, compliance with maritime regulations and the emergency response", plus whether "negligence, misconduct, dereliction of duty or institutional failures contributed". It also records that Ali said "the commissioners would determine their own procedures".

claims: Published Friday 31 July 2026, 2:07 AM GMT-4, bylined Staff Editor.

[SINGLE SOURCE] A joint opposition vigil of over two hours was held Thursday night outside Minister Juan Edghill's South Ruimveldt home, watched by police, demanding that Edghill and Minister Deodat Indar resign. Attendees included Azruddin Mohamed, APNU parliamentary leader Terrence Campbell, and MPs Odessa Primus, Vishnu Panday and Sherod Duncan.

[ALLEGATION] Mohamed alleged Captain Kevin Price "had been reluctant to make the ill-fated trip on July 18 as he was of the few that the vessel was overloaded", that at least five survivors would attest to this, that "the captain did not want to leave but received instructions to do so", and that the vessel "had already begun to take in water" as it left. These are untested claims advanced by a political figure about a man facing trial; they bear on his defence and must not be treated as established.

[ALLEGATION] Mohamed alleged that around 10pm on 18 July only one engine was working, making the vessel susceptible to overturning, and that although it capsized at 10.20pm it took the GDF Coast Guard seven hours to reach the scene.

[ALLEGATION] Mohamed alleged the GDF Coast Guard base at Pomeroon was "merely 20 minutes away from the point of capsizing" and criticised the response under Captain Shamsudeen; he repeated that two GDF helicopters were down.

[ALLEGATION] [SINGLE SOURCE] Mohamed "charged that there had been infighting in the government over who should get the $125m contract for the rehabilitation of the MV Barima and the task should have been finished before July 18." Unproven, and carried only here.

[ALLEGATION] Mohamed described the three charged men as "innocent" and accused the government of "slapping murder charges on three 'innocent' men from the T&HD", quoted as: "You put murder charges on three innocent men…I know y'all trying hard with me (to bring a murder charge) ..but I am one step ahead…". Note this is an assertion of innocence, not of guilt, but it is equally a pre-trial characterisation.
[SINGLE SOURCE] Mohamed vowed to support the families of the three charged men from his salary as Opposition Leader.

[ALLEGATION] Mohamed made personal claims about President Ali's wealth — "one of the richest presidents in the history of the Caribbean with a big farm at Long Creek and a monthly salary of $3m" — and asserted Vice President Bharrat Jagdeo "has not been happy with the way thing are going under President Irfaan Ali". Unevidenced.
The vigil is reported as putting the death toll at "over 70 lives".

sources.title: Assakata council wants MV Barima lifted, thorough probe
sources.summary: Published Friday 31 July 2026, 2:09 AM GMT-4, bylined Staff Editor. The Assakata Village Council (Region One) has formally called for recovery of the sunken vessel, an independent investigation, and resignations where responsibility is established. This is the first affected-community institutional position of its kind reported on 31 July. The resolutions followed a public meeting convened Wednesday by Toshao Terrence Domingo and councillors after their return from the 2026 National Toshaos Council Conference.
claims: Published Friday 31 July 2026, 2:09 AM GMT-4, bylined Staff Editor.

[SINGLE SOURCE] The Assakata Village Council (Region One) has formally called for recovery of the sunken vessel, an independent investigation, and resignations where responsibility is established. This is the first affected-community institutional position of its kind reported on 31 July.
The resolutions followed a public meeting convened Wednesday by Toshao Terrence Domingo and councillors after their return from the 2026 National Toshaos Council Conference.
The council is quoted: "Every life lost mattered and every family deserves truth, justice, and closure."
The council is quoted: "Our people deserve safe, reliable, and dignified transportation—not continued exposure to unacceptable risks."

Four specific demands: a thorough, transparent and independent investigation; accountability for every individual or institution found responsible; recovery of the MV Barima from the seabed "to facilitate what they described as a complete and credible investigation"; and immediate improvements to river transportation safety across Region One.
[SINGLE SOURCE] The council calls for the soldier from Whitewater Village who saved several people to receive a national honour and appropriate benefits.

The council thanked President Ali and the government alongside the GDF, GPF, the opposition, volunteers, boat operators and medical personnel — a notably non-partisan framing for a demand that includes ministerial resignations.

sources.title: Pres. Ali dodges media
sources.summary: Since returning to the country after the disaster, President Ali "has not faced the local media", relying on video statements while Prime Minister Mark Phillips has fronted the press briefings. No other 31 July item makes this cumulative point. "It should be noted that no invitation was extended to the local media to cover the ceremony" — the 30 July swearing-in at State House was closed to the press; proceedings were streamed on President Ali's Facebook page and the link later shared with media by Director of Publ
claims: [SINGLE SOURCE] Since returning to the country after the disaster, President Ali "has not faced the local media", relying on video statements while Prime Minister Mark Phillips has fronted the press briefings. No other 31 July item makes this cumulative point.

"It should be noted that no invitation was extended to the local media to cover the ceremony" — the 30 July swearing-in at State House was closed to the press; proceedings were streamed on President Ali's Facebook page and the link later shared with media by Director of Public Information Edward Layne.

Chairman Justice Godfrey Phillip Smith of Belize was sworn in virtually "as he is currently out of the jurisdiction"; the other four commissioners were sworn in person before Chief Magistrate Judy Latchman.

The COI is mandated to inspect "the condition and maintenance history of the vessel, including its seaworthiness" — which the article juxtaposes against the fact that "government mulls leaving the MV Barima on the seabed".
Ali is quoted: "Our nation deserves a full, fair and impartial account of what occurred, why it occurred and what must be done to ensure that such a tragedy is never repeated."
Death toll given as 73 confirmed dead and at least 30 still missing at sea.

sources.title: Let us not have to wait for a change of government for the MV Barima to be raised
sources.author: Janette Bulkan
sources.summary: The letter argues by analogy from the Prairie Green Landfill search in Manitoba, Canada, for the remains of murdered Indigenous women Morgan Harris and Marcedes Myran — a search initially refused, then funded at CAD 20 million by Premier Wab Kinew, which recovered remains in late February 2025. It cites the earlier federal study concluding a search "could take three years and cost up to CAD 184 million (USD 128 million)" — the cost argument that was ultimately overridden.
claims: The letter argues by analogy from the Prairie Green Landfill search in Manitoba, Canada, for the remains of murdered Indigenous women Morgan Harris and Marcedes Myran — a search initially refused, then funded at CAD 20 million by Premier Wab Kinew, which recovered remains in late February 2025.
It cites the earlier federal study concluding a search "could take three years and cost up to CAD 184 million (USD 128 million)" — the cost argument that was ultimately overridden.
It records the Manitoba Progressive Conservatives' formal apology in March 2025, quoting interim PC Leader Wayne Ewasko: "Our government erred. It's as simple as that."

[SINGLE SOURCE] The framing that raising the Barima may have to await a change of government — "please let us not have to await a change of government for the MV Barima to be raised" — is unique to this letter on 31 July.
The letter draws an explicit Indigenous-rights parallel, noting the Manitoba women "did not die while traveling in a State-owned and run ferry".

sources.title: Faulty design, weak foundation doomed Port Kaituma wharf from the start – Mahipaul
sources.summary: APNU MP Ganesh Mahipaul contends the Port Kaituma Wharf's structural problems originate in engineering error and inadequate site investigation before construction, not contractor failure. This is a political allegation, not an engineering finding. Mahipaul attributes design responsibility to Caribbean Engineering and Management Consultants Inc. (CEMCO), arguing the contractor merely built to supplied specifications. Mahipaul's specific technical claims — steel piles that failed to penetrate into firm ground and rem
claims: [ALLEGATION] APNU MP Ganesh Mahipaul contends the Port Kaituma Wharf's structural problems originate in engineering error and inadequate site investigation before construction, not contractor failure. This is a political allegation, not an engineering finding.
[ALLEGATION] Mahipaul attributes design responsibility to Caribbean Engineering and Management Consultants Inc. (CEMCO), arguing the contractor merely built to supplied specifications.

[SINGLE SOURCE] Mahipaul's specific technical claims — steel piles that failed to penetrate into firm ground and remained embedded in soft sediment; siting on former "Log Pond" land, a previous sawmill site containing buried debris; an oversized concrete retaining wall; improperly sized steel components; underestimated backfill calculations — are carried only in this account on 31 July.
Mahipaul is quoted: "Imagine trying to build a house on soft mud instead of solid ground. No matter how well you build it, it will eventually start to sink or fail."
Mahipaul is quoted: "The supports failed. Some of the steel tie rods snapped under the pressure."
The Port Kaituma project is stated as costing $1.4 billion and requiring substantial remedial work after structural movement, preventing the new MV Ma Lisha from docking.
[ALLEGATION] Mahipaul criticises CEMCO's continued receipt of major government contracts, including oversight of Gas-to-Energy infrastructure.

sources.title: Edghill and others must go
sources.author: Vishnu Prashad
sources.summary: The letter cites a Gazette Order dated 21 October 2025 assigning Minister of Public Works Juan Anthony Edghill responsibility for "Shipping and Harbour Services", and Cabinet Memorandum CP (2026) MOPW08/02 as the instrument under which he appointed the T&HD board. No other 31 July item cites these documents. The letter names the T&HD board as: Rosalinda Rasul (Chairperson, Head of Diaspora Affairs, Ministry of Foreign Affairs); Yurlander Hughes (former Personnel Manager, now Acting General Manager); Annaser Hamilto
claims: [SINGLE SOURCE] The letter cites a Gazette Order dated 21 October 2025 assigning Minister of Public Works Juan Anthony Edghill responsibility for "Shipping and Harbour Services", and Cabinet Memorandum CP (2026) MOPW08/02 as the instrument under which he appointed the T&HD board. No other 31 July item cites these documents.

[SINGLE SOURCE] The letter names the T&HD board as: Rosalinda Rasul (Chairperson, Head of Diaspora Affairs, Ministry of Foreign Affairs); Yurlander Hughes (former Personnel Manager, now Acting General Manager); Annaser Hamilton; Louise Williams (Director of Ports at MARAD); Indranauth Haralsingh; Dhanraj Singh; Jonathan LaCruz.

[ALLEGATION] It attacks the chairperson's record, asserting she was Country Manager of EZjet Air Services when the US Department of Transportation suspended its licences in November 2012. These are contested characterisations of a named private individual.

[SINGLE SOURCE] Financial claims: T&HD received in 2024 "GUY$1.2 billion in operational subsidies and GUY$5.1 billion in capital contributions", revenues of GUY$1.2 billion against employment costs of GUY$1.4 billion and fuel costs of GUY$1.3 billion, sourced to the Ministry of Finance website.

Demands: that Edghill and Hughes "vacate their positions until the Independent Commission of Inquiry complete its work", and that the entire board be "sacked for abandonment of oversight, failure of duty of care, and ineffective corporate governance".

[CONTRADICTS ARCHIVE] The letter opens by saying the vessel capsized "off the Pomeroon River with some 100 Guyanese dying". The archive figure is ~103 dead or missing, with 73 bodies recovered on the domestic count and about 30 unaccounted for; "some 100 dying" conflates the recovered and the missing.

sources.title: Don't Bury the Truth
sources.summary: Editorial position: the wreck must be raised. "The MV Barima is no ordinary shipwreck. It is a potential crime scene." The paper charges a government reversal: after initially pledging recovery and closure, the administration moved to leaving the ferry on the seabed as a memorial, then — after Opposition Leader Azruddin Mohamed offered to finance a salvage — announced that families would decide. "That abrupt reversal raises a troubling question. If salvage was always an option, why now it is left to the families to
claims: Editorial position: the wreck must be raised. "The MV Barima is no ordinary shipwreck. It is a potential crime scene."

The paper charges a government reversal: after initially pledging recovery and closure, the administration moved to leaving the ferry on the seabed as a memorial, then — after Opposition Leader Azruddin Mohamed offered to finance a salvage — announced that families would decide. "That abrupt reversal raises a troubling question. If salvage was always an option, why now it is left to the families to decide."
"Every day that the vessel remains underwater increases the possibility that crucial evidence deteriorates or disappears forever."
"To knowingly leave perhaps the most important exhibit on the ocean floor risks reducing the inquiry to an exercise built on incomplete facts."
"Government insists it has 'nothing to hide.' If that is indeed so, then recovering the MV Barima should strengthen, not weaken its position."

The editorial notes Transparency Institute Guyana Inc.'s position that appointing foreign commissioners alone does not make an inquiry independent if key stakeholders were excluded from its formation.
"A memorial has its place. But memorials are built after every reasonable effort has been exhausted—not before."

sources.title: Congregational Union hopes for speedy convening of MV Barima COI
sources.summary: The Guyana Congregational Union, in a statement issued Wednesday, extends condolences and says it hopes the newly appointed Commission will begin its work "very soon". The Union says it "trusts the panel's eventual findings and recommendations will bring some degree of comfort and satisfaction" to families and the wider public. The Union characterises the loss as unprecedented — Guyana has never suffered such a catastrophic loss of life in a single incident — and dwells on the deaths of young people and children.

The Union says it "trusts the panel's eventual findings and recommendations will bring some degree of comfort and satisfaction" to families and the wider public.

sources.title: OGGN Oil Talk — Beyond the MV Barima ferry wreck: suggestions for sea and river transport systems in Guyana
sources.outlet: OGGN Oil Talk (Oil and Gas Governance Network), via Kaieteur Radio Guyana
sources.author: Host: Janette Bulkan. Guest: David Patterson
sources.summary: A one-hour OGGN Oil Talk podcast streamed live on 30 July on the Kaieteur Radio Guyana channel, hosted by Janette Bulkan with David Patterson, AFC shadow minister for public works and a former Minister of Public Works. Patterson, having held the ministry, treats annual certification of these vessels as routine — "how can you say you don't have the registration certificate... but you are certifying it every year" — which bears directly on the certificate no one has produced. He states the Transport and Harbours Department has not turned a profit since 2007 or 2009 and has not been officially audited since about 2005-2006. He cites Cap. 49:07 s. 18, under which inspectors of shipping may prevent overloaded vessels sailing and detain unfit ones. He argues the murder charges hollow out the inquiry because the operator's own management will also decline to self-incriminate, and predicts masters may refuse to sail. Bulkan puts the rescue timeline directly: first rescue at 2:27 a.m., more than three hours on. Auto-caption source; 92 per cent of the programme captured.
claims: PROGRAMME. A one-hour podcast, streamed live on 30 July 2026 on the Kaieteur Radio Guyana channel, 734 views at retrieval. Host Janette Bulkan; guest David Patterson, shadow minister for public works for the Alliance For Change and a former Minister of Public Works. Stated topic: "beyond the MV Barima ferry wreck, suggestions for sea and river transport systems in Guyana." OGGN describes itself as founded in 2017, a registered 501(c)(3) non-profit in New York, and "fiercely independent with no political affiliations."

[SINGLE SOURCE — and directly on the certificate this archive has been unable to find] Patterson, a former Minister of Public Works, states that these vessels are certified annually and compares the process to a road-fitness certificate: "how can you say you don't have the registration certificate of a document... but you are certifying it every year." He adds that speed boats and cargo boats renew their licences at MARAD every year, and that a survey may be partial rather than a full check. If correct, an annual certification record should exist for the Barima.

[SINGLE SOURCE] Patterson states that the Transport and Harbours Department "has not turned a profit since 2007 or 2009", and that it has not been officially audited by the Auditor General's office since "most likely I think 2005, 2006". This archive has separately recorded that no Auditor General finding specific to the T&HD could be located; this is a former minister asserting that no official audit has been done for roughly two decades. Unverified.

STATUTORY POWERS THAT WERE AVAILABLE. Patterson cites the Shipping Casualties Investigation and Prevention Act, Cap. 49:07, and states that under section 18 inspectors of shipping have "sweeping powers": to board vessels, inspect machinery and equipment, examine certificates, "prevent overloaded vessels from sailing", and detain any vessel unfit for a voyage, with power to remove excess cargo or passengers. He is describing powers that existed before 18 July.

[SINGLE SOURCE — extends the self-incrimination problem well beyond the three accused] Patterson argues the murder charges will hollow out the Commission of Inquiry, because the operator's management will also decline to answer: the marine superintendent "is not going to incriminate himself", nor the chief engineer responsible for the vessels, "nor would the general manager of transport and harbours". On his account the inquiry is left with "circumstantial" evidence and "he say, she say".

[SINGLE SOURCE] Patterson states a consequence for the service itself: "every captain now on any one of these vessels... may refuse to work", because the charges establish that a captain is ultimately responsible "irrespective of whatever orders you have" and can be charged with murder. He predicts push-back from masters. Bulkan puts the same point as a long-term risk to indigenous and business travel on a route with no road alternative.

THE RESCUE TIMELINE, PUT DIRECTLY. Bulkan states that on the Prime Minister's own account the first rescue "took place at 27 minutes past 2 on Sunday, that's more than 3 hours later", with the vessel down roughly seven to ten miles from shore, and asks what is made of a gap of "two and a half hours, no rescue". This is the sharpest published statement of the rescue-timeline question in this corpus.

[SINGLE SOURCE] Patterson describes the pre-departure procedure he says applied: a travel plan is issued before sailing, and the "lighthouse", which he calls the maritime nerve centre, together with the harbour master, is supposed to check it. He states that on a Mayday the lighthouse holds a shipping chart showing vessels off the coast and would radio a vessel within five or ten nautical miles — and that nothing of the kind has been heard about in this case.

[SINGLE SOURCE] Patterson names Michael Tenant as a former harbour master who he says was a stickler for procedure, states that Tenant resigned in January after a brief meeting with new ministers, and says he spoke to him within the last few days.
[SINGLE SOURCE] On flares, Patterson notes accounts that flares were seen but says nobody has established who saw them or when.

[SINGLE SOURCE] Patterson describes controls he says were instituted during his own tenure: an additional inspectorate layer to double-check passengers and cargo, because MARAD's technical regulatory inspection was checking only whether a load was under 100 tons. He describes ticket touting — a family of ten buying all ten tickets and reselling — as a problem the extra layer was meant to stop, and says that unit was hired directly through the Transport and Harbours Department rather than through MARAD.

[SINGLE SOURCE] Patterson states that under his policy a dedicated fuel barge carried fuel to Region One weekly, and that cargo for construction and mining was not permitted on the passenger vessels because space and weight were limited. He argues for separating cargo barges from passenger ferries, and for short hops from Charity or Supenaam rather than 18-to-24-hour voyages.

MARINE SAFETY INVESTIGATION, RELAYED. Bulkan relays MP Amanza Walton-Desir's argument that a marine safety investigation under SOLAS and the IMO is mandatory, cannot be substituted by a Commission of Inquiry, and must be independent of the state because the state is regulator, certifying authority, inspecting authority and operator at once — so it "must be capable of commanding public confidence". This corroborates the joint opposition objection already recorded in this corpus.

[SINGLE SOURCE] On the MSRC. Bulkan asks why information came from the Prime Minister and the Ministry of Public Works rather than from the professional staff of the Maritime Search and Rescue Coordination Centre, whose function is to coordinate rescue and report to the public. Patterson answers that the government "by default they clamp down on information" and "like to control the entire information space", and describes how a functioning centre would work: all bodies in one room, one verified figure, and a designated liaison briefing families at regular intervals. He states search and rescue was moved and coordinated under the Civil Defence Commission.

[SINGLE SOURCE — offers an explanation for a figure jump this archive has recorded] Patterson attributes an early jump in the survivor count to counting being split between bodies: he says survivors picked up by a different body were not counted, so the numbers moved. He offers this as an example of what a single coordinating centre would have prevented.

A WIDER MISSING RANGE THAN THIS ARCHIVE CARRIES. Bulkan frames the toll as 76 survivors and 73 bodies retrieved, and says of those unaccounted for "probably between 30 and 50. We still do not know how many persons are unaccounted for." Almost every other source in this corpus gives about 30. Recorded as a divergence, not adopted.

[ALLEGATION — relaying the account of an accused man who has not been tried] Patterson relays the captain's reported account that the vessel had no functioning anchor, no search-and-rescue transponder and no emergency position-indicating radio beacon, and that the life rafts had not been certified for four years. This archive does not adopt it.

CONTEXT RAISED. Bulkan refers to the Mahdia dormitory fire of three years earlier, in which she says twenty girls in the care of the state died, as a prior mass-casualty event involving indigenous people. Patterson argues against "treating the indigenous communities as byproducts".

NOT REACHED. Bulkan's opening agenda listed the role of ExxonMobil and Chevron in Guyana's marine space, which she said had been "largely silent", plus the treatment of Guyanese journalists, the role of fishers and self-care for medical personnel. The captured portion does not reach a substantive discussion of the oil companies.

sources.title: Ministry lists its cargo on MV Barima
sources.author: Staff Editor
sources.summary: ENTIRELY NEW TO THE RECORD: the Ministry of Public Works has, for the first time, published an itemised list of its own consigned cargo aboard the MV Barima on the fatal voyage. The Ministry's statement, quoted: "Please be advised, the Ministry of Public Works wishes to inform the public that the consigned cargo aboard the MV Barima, on the Ministry's behalf, at the time of the July 18 Departure, is as follows." The list is: "One Honda Side-by-Side ATV"; "Six Drums of Gasoline"; "Four Drums of Diesel."

The list is: "One Honda Side-by-Side ATV"; "Six Drums of Gasoline"; "Four Drums of Diesel."
The disclosure was made "yesterday" — i.e. 29 July 2026.
The Ministry acted "under pressure over how much of its cargo had been on the MV Barima on July 18th when it capsized and killed more than 70 persons."

The list is a statement by the Ministry about its own consignment only; it is not a manifest, is not audited, and says nothing about total cargo aboard or about stowage. It should not be read as a finding on loading.

claims: First institutional editorial in the corpus framing the resignation question as a constitutional test rather than a political one.

"Yet despite the intensity of those calls, neither Minister nor the President has responded in any meaningful way." As at 30 July this is the state of the record: Edghill's 29 July "appropriate time" remark is the only ministerial response.

"Is the Government attempting to save Juan Edghill, or is it attempting to protect a much broader principle—that ministers will remain politically insulated regardless of the failures that occur within their portfolios?"

The editorial states the jurisdictional position: "The Ministry of Public Works exercises responsibility for Guyana's maritime transport infrastructure through the Transport and Harbours Department, the agency charged with administering and regulating state-owned vessels."
"Political accountability is not the same as criminal or civil liability. A minister is not expected to resign because he personally caused an accident."

"On previous occasions involving ministerial controversy or significant failures within government, he has consistently chosen caution over decisive intervention… Silence, when repeated often enough, becomes policy."
"The issue is no longer confined to whether Juan Edghill or Deodat Indar should resign. It is whether the Presidency remains committed to the constitutional principle that ministers are accountable."

sources.title: Who's responsible, who will take responsibility?
sources.author: GHK Lall
sources.summary: "According to news reports of Saturday, 73 bodies have been recovered and 76 rescued. Taking the official count of 179 passengers on board the MV Barima, it means that 30 of them are still unaccounted for." Lall does the same arithmetic the archive does and reaches the same place. "Over a week after the disaster, there is still uncertainty about how many passengers, paying or not, with a ticket or lacking one, were onboard the vessel."

"The people under whose watch that disaster occurred have one clear duty in front of them. Man or woman, they have to go."
He identifies the parallel he considers dangerous: "Providing inaccurate information, minimizing loss, shifting blame, targeting dissenters, and massive corruption in the background."

sources.title: The MV Barima and the Maritime Statute Book of Guyana: A Fully Expanded Analysis of Statutory Deficiency in the Law Governing Domestic Passenger Shipping
sources.outlet: Robert C. Millington (submitted to this archive by the author)
sources.author: Robert C. Millington
sources.summary: A 253-page statutory analysis submitted to this archive by its author, Robert C. Millington - a retired US Navy officer and former licensed US Coast Guard Merchant Marine Deck Officer and First Class Ship Pilot, both Unlimited Tonnage. Read from the authorised Laws of Guyana, it argues that Guyana's maritime statute book contains almost no enforceable safety standard for the class of vessel most Guyanese travel on, requires nobody to count who goes aboard, and imposes on no person a duty to investigate a marine casualty. Its central finding is a 24-metre gap: the only instrument containing stability criteria, muster requirements and a record of passengers applies to vessels under 24 metres, while the survey instrument covering vessels above 24 metres excludes passenger ships in five words - so the Barima at 40.26 metres fell under neither. It also explains why a load line cannot answer the overloading question, why the Commission sits under a general statute rather than a maritime one, and identifies a six-month limitation period against the operator expiring on or about 18 January 2027. It makes no finding of fact and presumes the innocence of everyone charged.
claims: A 253-page statutory analysis by Robert C. Millington - retired United States Navy naval officer, former licensed US Coast Guard Merchant Marine Deck Officer (Unlimited Tonnage) and former First Class Ship Pilot (Unlimited Tonnage), BSc Marine Transportation, State University of New York Maritime College at Fort Schuyler, thirty-nine years in the military, maritime and logistics sectors. Submitted as an aid to the Commission of Inquiry. Text current to 29 July 2026

Statutory text read directly from the authorised Laws of Guyana, Revised Edition, as authorised by L.R.O. 1/2012, covering Cap. 49:01 (Guyana Shipping Act), Cap. 49:04 (Transport and Harbours Act), Cap. 49:07 (Shipping Casualties (Investigation and Prevention) Act 1883), Cap. 50:01 (River Navigation Act 1891) and Cap. 47:01

THE 24-METRE GAP - the central finding. The Barima was 40.26 m long. Because she exceeded 24 metres the Guyana Shipping (Small Commercial Ship Safety) Regulations, Reg. 5 of 2005 did not apply to her - and that instrument is 'the only place in the entire 904-page consolidation containing intact stability criteria, stability information for operating personnel, an ISM-referenced safety management system, a Record of Passengers, a marine casualty notification duty, and station bill, muster and drill requirements'

Because she was a passenger ship the Guyana Shipping (Cargo Ship Survey) Regulations, Reg. 6 of 2005 expressly carved her out: regulation 3 applies to sea-going Guyana ships of less than 500 gross tonnage but above 24 metres in length 'except passenger ships, fishing vessels and pleasure craft'. In the author's words she 'fell squarely inside the band and was removed from it by five words'

Part XV of Cap. 49:01, headed 'Passenger Ships', consists of two sections - one an enabling power to make regulations that do not appear in the authorised consolidation, the other creating offences of drunkenness and fare evasion

The author's summary of the consequence: 'A vessel one metre shorter, carrying a small fraction of her complement, was subject to a materially more demanding safety code than she was. Had she carried freight instead of people, she would have been subject to a five-yearly structural and machinery survey and to annual surveys. Because she carried people, she was subject to neither instrument'

NO COUNTING DUTY EXISTS. SOLAS Chapter III regulation 27 requires all persons on board a passenger ship to be counted before departure and the record kept ashore. Cap. 49:01 s. 398(1)(b) confers a power to require particulars as to all passengers but is an enabling power with no regulations made under it. The author's conclusion: 'The discrepancy between 133 and 179 is therefore not, on the face of the statute book, a breach of any counting duty - because no counting duty exists.' A manifest is described as a commercial document compiled from bookings for revenue purposes, not a safety document

THE LOAD LINE CANNOT ANSWER THE OVERLOADING QUESTION, and the author locates the fault in the statute rather than in the regulator: 'A load line measures reserve buoyancy at a given displacement. It measures total weight and water density. It is entirely indifferent to where that weight is.' It does not measure metacentric height, the righting-lever curve, the area under that curve, the angle of vanishing stability, free-surface effect, the downflooding angle, passenger crowding, or whether the vessel is already taking water. 'Every one of those determines whether a vessel capsizes. Not one is measured by the mark on her side'

On why MARAD used it: 'the load line is the only quantitative loading control Guyanese law gives for this class of vessel. There are no intact stability criteria, no prescribed content for stability information under s. 290, no duty to calculate a departure condition, no approved loading conditions, and no passenger-crowding criterion. A regulator with a load line and nothing else will use the load line'

THE OWNER IS THE REGULATOR. Cap. 49:01 s. 3(3) provides that where a Guyana Government ship is registered, 'any reference to an owner shall be construed as a reference to the Director'. The owner must report accidents to the Director (s. 237), notify defects to the Director (s. 292), carry stability information (s. 290), not send an unseaworthy ship to sea (s. 337), and is subject to detention by the Director (s. 339). 'In every case the person who must report is the person to whom the report is made.' The same Director appoints the assessors to any Board of formal investigation (s. 429(1)) and receives its report (s. 429(6))

TWO CASUALTY-INVESTIGATION REGIMES, NEITHER OF WHICH COULD LAWFULLY BE USED. Cap. 49:01 Part XVIII (1998) gives the Minister a power and not a duty - 'no threshold, no trigger, no time limit, no duty to publish'. Cap. 49:07 Part I (1883) provides at s. 3 that nothing in that Part applies to any ship belonging to or in the service of the State; the Barima belonged to the State, so 'the machinery was disapplied to her by its own terms'. The author states the Commission of Inquiry therefore correctly sits under the general Commissions of Inquiry Act, and that this is 'the clearest possible proof of the deficiency'

The IMO Casualty Investigation Code, mandatory under SOLAS Chapter XI-1 regulation 6 since 1 January 2010, is described as unimplemented in Guyana in every respect - no mandatory investigation of a very serious marine casualty, no independence, no separation from blame attribution, no protection for witness evidence, no duty to publish, no submission to the IMO

THE PENALTIES ARE INVERTED. Submerging a load line, Cap. 49:01 s. 319: $100,000. Fraudulently altering draught marks, Cap. 49:04 s. 46: $48,750. Sailing with no stability information, s. 290(3): $10,000. Sending a ship to sea so unseaworthy that life is likely to be endangered, s. 337 via s. 444(1): $25,000 and six months. 'A vessel loaded one centimetre too deep attracts four times the fine of a vessel sent to sea in a condition likely to kill everyone aboard.' Both Acts supply a defence that sending an unseaworthy ship to sea was 'reasonable and justifiable'

The author records - expressing no view on the charges and presuming innocence - that 'the recourse to common-law murder is a direct consequence of the penalty structure of the Guyana Shipping Act - a legislative failure, not a prosecutorial choice'

ACCOUNTABILITY REACHES ONLY CERTIFICATE HOLDERS. Cap. 49:01 s. 429(3) permits a Board of formal investigation to cancel or suspend a certificate or censure its holder, and the author states 'that is the whole of its dispositive power over persons'. There is no finding available against a company, a Government Department, a Ministry, MARAD, the Director, or any uncertificated person; the Transport and Harbours Department 'cannot commit an offence under the Act, because the Act creates none capable of being committed by a Department'. His conclusion: 'Under the maritime statutes as they stand, the small man is the only person the law can reach'

THE SUPERINTENDENT OF LOADING DOES NOT EXIST IN LAW - recorded as Deficiency 62. The office the Minister publicly identified as responsible for inspection and loading 'is not created by, named in, or given any duty by' Cap. 49:01, Cap. 49:04, Cap. 49:07 or Cap. 50:01. No qualification is prescribed for it, no standard governs how it loads, no record is required and no offence attaches to it. 'A person cannot be regulated by an office the statute does not create.' The author notes one of the three men charged on 28 July is described as the Goods or Loading Superintendent

THE STATUTE STILL POINTS AT THE UNITED KINGDOM. Cap. 49:07 s. 5(4) requires the Minister to transmit a court of inquiry's report to 'the Board of Trade of the Government of the United Kingdom', as amended in 1998. The Coasting and Passenger Trade Regulations reg. 13(3) provide that the number of passengers a coasting steam vessel may carry is 'as ascertained in accordance with the survey established from time to time by the Board of Trade of the United Kingdom' - which the author states is the only rule in Guyanese law for ascertaining the passenger capacity of a power-driven coasting vessel. The Fourth Schedule prices the exercise at $20 for a vessel over 120 feet by deck measurement; the Barima was 126.5 feet

THE 1891 RIVER LAW IS BETTER THAN THE 1998 SEA LAW. The River Navigation Regulations under Cap. 50:01 require annual inspection, branded waterlines against a statutory freeboard scale, machinery and steering maintained on pain of detention, a certificated maximum number of persons crew included with that number painted on both bows, one lifebelt for every certificated person, a count of persons entered in a book at a Government Station before departure, a prohibition on taking any additional person aboard after reporting, and a duty to report any accident whatever occasioning loss of life

Regulation 19(1), made in 1918, permits one passenger with baggage for every five square feet of deck surface, expressly excluding space occupied by machinery, open hatches, skylights, fuel and any cargo carried on deck - a self-executing deck-area capacity rule that automatically reduces the permitted number of persons as deck cargo is loaded. The author states it applies on the Barima River and the Kaituma Creek but not on the sea passage between them and Georgetown

Cap. 50:01 s. 14, inserted in 1998, is described as the only mandatory enforcement duty in the entire Guyanese maritime statute book: 'it shall be the duty of the Director and the Maritime Administration Department to enforce' the Act. 'In 1998 Parliament knew how to write such a duty. It wrote one, once, into an 1891 river statute, and did not write it into the new Act'

WHAT THE REGULATOR SAID SEVEN YEARS BEFORE THE CASUALTY, which the author calls the most significant single item of institutional evidence in the document because it predates and is therefore uncontaminated by the casualty. On 27 March 2019 the Director General of MARAD, Claudette Rogers, stated publicly that 'although Guyana has ratified the main International Maritime Conventions, the requisite regulations need to be enacted or put in place because the country follows the common law system'; that the IMO Member State Audit of Guyana was completed in 2018; that one necessary measure arising directly from that audit was 'the enacting of regulations to give full and complete effect to the conventions which Guyana has ratified'; that Professor Duke Pollard, a retired Judge of the Caribbean Court of Justice, had been retained to update Guyana's maritime legislation and had completed the assignment with recommendations expressly directed at eliminating conflicts among agencies as to where responsibility for key maritime functions resides; and that Guyana had not ratified the STCW 95 amendments while Guyanese surveyors were issuing certificates on that basis, which she described as a significant breach of international maritime law

The author identifies four documents which he says will very largely answer the Commission's question about institutional failure, and which all exist: the IMO Member State Audit report, Guyana's corrective action plan, the progress reports on its implementation, and the Pollard report and recommendations

THE 18 JANUARY 2027 LIMITATION DEADLINE - recorded as the most urgent item in the document. Cap. 49:04 s. 23 requires that no action against the Transport and Harbours Department be commenced until one month after written notice naming the claimant's legal practitioner has been served, and that every such action be commenced within six months after the thing done or omitted, 'and not otherwise'. Six months from 18 July 2026 expires on or about 18 January 2027; notice must therefore be served by on or about 18 December 2026

Six reasons the author gives for why that period is a trap for the people least able to avoid it: it runs from the act or omission and not from knowledge, death, identification of a body or a grant of representation; the Commission will very probably not have reported within six months, so a family that waits may find the period gone; claimants are disproportionately Region One residents with no road to Georgetown and the vessel that connected them is on the seabed; the notice must name a practitioner, so a family must find and instruct one before the clock can be stopped; five recovered victims remained unidentified and at least thirty unaccounted for as at 27 July 2026, and a family with no body and no death certificate cannot readily obtain a grant of representation while s. 23 makes no allowance; and ex gratia assistance is not compensation and does not stop the clock

AND THERE IS NO INSURER TO CLAIM AGAINST. Cap. 49:01 s. 398(2) requires the Minister to have due regard to the Athens Convention when making passenger-ship regulations; no such regulations were made, 'so the requirement of due regard never attached to anything'. Guyana enacted the limitation of liability in Part XVI and not the liability - 'the protective half of the international bargain was omitted and the limiting half retained'. There is no strict liability for a shipping incident, no presumed fault, no compulsory insurance and no direct right of action against an insurer

[CONFLICT WITH THIS ARCHIVE] The document gives the distress signal as 22:43, against the 23:01 this archive records from the Department of Public Information and the BBC. The author further states that on the night 'the distress signal reached an aviation authority at 22:43 and took twenty minutes, through two intermediaries, to reach the maritime rescue authority' - which, if correct, reconciles the two times and explains why several outlets named air traffic control as the recipient
The author states that the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre has no statutory existence and that the SAR Convention 1979 is unimplemented in Guyana

Vessel particulars given: 284 grt / 111 nrt; 40.26 m x 8.87 m; draft 7.5 ft; twin screw; Ferguson Brothers (Port Glasgow) Ltd, yard no. 340; launched 9 May 1939; registered Georgetown 17 November 1939. Life-saving equipment given as 250 lifejackets, 6 inflatable liferafts and 2 rigid liferafts. Region One (Barima-Waini) population given as 38,956 at the 2022 census, with no road to Georgetown

The author records certificated capacity as given variously as approximately 397, approximately 394 and approximately 150 passengers by three named sources, and states that on the manifest figure of 133 'the arithmetic does not close at all: 76 rescued plus 73 recovered dead exceeds 133 by sixteen'

DEFICIENCY COUNT: 87 numbered deficiencies plus 20 unnumbered structural items - 42 CRITICAL, 29 HIGH, 11 MEDIUM, 3 LOW and 2 URGENT-TIME. Chapter 11 sets each against its provision, the gap, the MV Barima nexus, an international benchmark and a recommended reform

COMPARATIVE FINDING: the MV Christena, lost off St Kitts and Nevis on 1 August 1970 with 233 dead, was built between 1958 and 1959 by Sprostons Ltd in Georgetown, British Guiana. The Renwick Commission of Inquiry, also constituted under a Commissions of Inquiry Act, heard 45 witnesses and reported in October 1970, about ten weeks after the loss. It found the vessel dangerously overloaded and improperly loaded, and no reliable system for counting passengers before departure; she had sailed with her ballast tanks empty as standard practice, adopted so she would ride higher and passengers would stop complaining about spray

Across Christena (1970), Dona Paz (1987), Bukoba (1996), Le Joola (2002) and Sewol (2014) the author identifies recurring causal factors - certificated capacity exceeded; no reliable count of persons; improper cargo loading; insufficient ballast; a known defect not acted upon; modification raising the centre of gravity; closures unsecured; slow rescue; and a lifeline route with no alternative - and states that every one maps to a Guyanese deficiency identified in the document

TEN RECOMMENDED REFORMS, which the author states require no new Act because the regulation-making powers already exist under Cap. 49:01 ss. 251, 398 and 452 or Cap. 49:07 s. 25: a domestic passenger vessel safety code for all vessels of 24 metres and over based on the IMO Model Regulations on Domestic Ferry Safety; a published maximum number of persons marked on the vessel with exceeding it an offence by the carrier; a duty to count every person at embarkation with no boarding after the count closes; prescribed content for stability information with the departure condition calculated, recorded and certified before every voyage; an independent permanent multi-modal Transport Safety Board reporting to Parliament; repeal of s. 3(3) so the regulator is no longer the owner; repeal of the 'reasonable and justifiable' defence; accession to the Athens Convention 2002 Protocol; dealing with Cap. 49:04 s. 23 before 18 January 2027; and a Maritime Search and Rescue Act

STATED LIMITATIONS, which the author discloses rather than conceals: the consolidation relied on is current only to L.R.O. 1/2012, so every finding expressed as the absence of a regulation is subject to verification against post-2012 instruments and the Official Gazette; and Guyana's accession status could not be verified instrument by instrument against the IMO Status of Conventions table, which he lists as Priority One verification item number one

The author states the document 'is not an accident investigation; it has no access to the wreck, the certificates, the stability book, the manifest or any witness', is not a submission that any particular provision was breached, is not a criticism of the individuals who administer the Guyanese maritime system, and makes no finding of fact. Every person charged, detained, suspended or named is expressly presumed innocent

The author corrects his own earlier drafts in two respects recorded in the document: an earlier framing of the owner-regulator problem as a single-ministry fusion of operator and regulator was wrong, because MARAD and the Transport and Harbours Department sit under different Ministers, and the real defect is narrower and lies inside the office of the Director; and an earlier draft recorded that the text of Cap. 49:07 could not be obtained, which has since been resolved

sources.title: Murder is not limited to intentional killing
sources.author: Roopnauth Hardyal
sources.summary: A letter to the editor answering Nigel Hughes's intent argument directly, though without naming him: "The proposition that a charge of murder can only arise where it is proven that an accused person intended to kill or intended to inflict grievous bodily harm, knowing that death was the likely consequence is, at best, incomplete and, at worst, misleading." Argues for extreme-recklessness murder: "Where it can be established beyond a reasonable doubt that an individual acted with extreme recklessness or what is often described as a 'depraved indifference' or 'wanton disregard' for human life, the requisite mental.
claims: A letter to the editor answering Nigel Hughes's intent argument directly, though without naming him: "The proposition that a charge of murder can only arise where it is proven that an accused person intended to kill or intended to inflict grievous bodily harm, knowing that death was the likely consequence is, at best, incomplete and, at worst, misleading."

Argues for extreme-recklessness murder: "Where it can be established beyond a reasonable doubt that an individual acted with extreme recklessness or what is often described as a 'depraved indifference' or 'wanton disregard' for human life, the requisite mental element for murder may be satisfied."
Concedes the standard is high: "However, in this instance the evidence must satisfy an exceptionally high threshold."

"The law is concerned not only with what a person hopes will happen but also with what that person knowingly risks. A conscious decision to proceed in the face of an obvious probability of death may demonstrate such contempt for human life that the distinction between recklessness and intent becomes legally insignificant."

"To insist that only a proven intention to kill can justify a murder charge ignores the fact that in the most egregious cases, extreme recklessness may itself supply the malice that the law requires."

Closing pointed question on the chain of responsibility: "And as an aside, did one local commentator not characterise, in a cavalier fashion, the sinking of the M.V. Barima as a mass killing. If so, who is the first in the chain of culpability?"
GENRE NOTE: this is a signed letter, not reporting. It supplies the corpus's only sustained legal argument FOR the availability of a murder charge on these facts.

Wade on scope: "Is the institution of murder charges having the effect of shielding senior officials from closer scrutiny by focusing public attention almost exclusively on the Captain and crew? That is a question the Guyanese people are entitled to ask."

STATUTORY BASIS — new and specific: Ram argues "the Commission should have been established under Part XVIII of the Shipping Act, which provides for a statutory marine investigation chaired by a sitting judge or magistrate with powers to compel evidence and suspend or revoke maritime certificates where negligence is found." Ram calls for Minister Edghill and the MARAD Director General "to step aside while the inquiry proceeds and to testify before the Commission."

Ram urges that all Barima documents — "maintenance records, surveys, manifests, inspection reports, and files concerning the Kalliopi N and Ma Lisha — are immediately secured to prevent alteration or destruction," warning they "could form key evidence in future civil lawsuits by grieving families."

Ram: "A new ship sat at her moorings waiting for you. In its stead, an old one sailed without you and did not come back, with more than one hundred innocent and unsuspecting lives lost," and "This one must serve the dead and not you, your Administration or your party."

It also carries an asset count of 17 — 14 vessels and three aircraft — against 18 in the Prime Minister's release of the same day, a small unreconciled divergence between two government releases published hours apart.

The obstacles given are limited visibility from a muddy seabed, strong tidal currents near the river mouth, and shallow water complicating visual search.
The deployment is described as 17 primary assets — 14 vessels and three aircraft — with specialised local and international dive teams.
[CONTESTED] The asset count of **17** here sits against **18** in the Prime Minister's release of the same day. Both are state releases dated 28 July. Neither reconciles the other.

This is the first first-hand account in this corpus from a diver's side of the conditions later cited in support of leaving the wreck in place, and it is dated one day *before* the French team's assessment of 27 July was reported.

sources.title: After-action report to review MV Barima rescue operation once mission concludes

It establishes that such a record exists and is to be analysed, which is different from the absence the archive had recorded. What it does not establish is that anyone outside the GDF will see it: the release sets no deadline, names no recipient, and gives no undertaking to publish.

It establishes that a tasking and communications record for the night of 18-19 July **exists and is to be analysed** — which this archive had recorded only as an absence in published journalism.

sources.title: Pres. Ali to unveil 5-member Int'l COI today to probe MV Barima disaster
sources.summary: Kaieteur News reports that President Irfaan Ali is expected to announce a five-member commission of inquiry on 26 July, one week after the MV Barima capsized. It sets out the scope Ali announced on Saturday 25 July: vessel loading, boarding procedures, seaworthiness, maintenance history, compliance with maritime law, conduct of master and crew, lifesaving arrangements, weather, and a review of the search and rescue response. The commission is to be empowered to find negligence, misconduct, dereliction of duty or institutional failure and to recommend reforms. The report carries the first detailed opposition rejections, from Azruddin Mohamed and APNU, over non-consultation and the retention of Ministers Edghill and Indar.
claims: President Irfaan Ali is expected to announce a five-member commission on 26 July to probe the 18 July capsizing of the MV Barima, which has so far claimed 73 lives.
Ali said in a statement on Saturday afternoon that the commission will be named in keeping with his commitment to an 'international and independent' commission of inquiry.

Ali said the commission will comprise experts in law, marine engineering, maritime safety and disaster investigation, 'carefully selected for their independence, technical expertise, and proven ability'.
The Commission will be responsible for determining its own procedures and method of work, according to the President.

The Commission will examine loading of the vessel, passenger boarding procedures, conditions on board, seaworthiness, maintenance history, compliance with maritime laws and safety standards, conduct and competence of the master and crew, passenger management and lifesaving arrangements, and the role of weather and sea conditions.
The Commission will review the search, rescue and recovery operations, assessing adequacy, coordination and effectiveness of the response by all agencies.
The Commission will be empowered to determine whether negligence, misconduct, dereliction of duty, or institutional failures contributed to or caused the tragedy.
Opposition Leader Azruddin Mohamed said neither he nor any parliamentary opposition party was consulted in establishing the Commission.

Mohamed said Ministers Juan Edghill (Public Works) and Deodat Indar (Public Utilities and Aviation), whose ministries have responsibility for MARAD and the THD, should be recused from any involvement while the inquiry is ongoing and should be required to appear before the Commission.

Mohamed, leader of the We Invest in Nationhood (WIN) party, said reports for previous COIs have been hidden from the public and called for the full inquiry to be livestreamed and the full final report released.
Mohamed suggested Guyana, as an IMO member, should seek the involvement of international maritime experts and institutions.
APNU expressed concern that the President did not send Ministers Edghill and Indar on administrative leave pending the outcome of the inquiry.
APNU said the Commission was selected solely by the Head of State, contrary to widespread calls from civil society and the opposition for an inclusive process.
APNU said excluding the opposition 'creates the unfortunate perception that this exercise is designed to manage public outrage rather than establish the full truth'.

APNU reiterated calls for Edghill and Indar to be sent home, for meaningful consultation with the opposition on commission members and terms of reference, and for full public disclosure of maintenance records, inspection reports and communications relating to the MV Barima.

sources.title: Other nations' ministers stepped down following deadly ferry disasters
sources.summary: A 26 July Kaieteur News compendium of the organised demands for Minister Juan Edghill's resignation, set against international precedent. It records that on 19 July Edghill gave figures of 284 tonnes licensed cargo against 268 tonnes manifested and 397 licensed passengers against 116 aboard, then conceded the next day that the manifest did not reflect the number of people on board. It is the piece that identifies the statutory basis being proposed: the AFC called for a Commission of Inquiry under the Commission of Inquiry Act, Chapter 19:03. It sets out ministerial resignation precedents after ferry disasters in Gabon (2023), South Korea (2014) and Senegal (2002).
claims: On July 19 Minister Juan Edghill said the MV Barima was licensed to carry 284 tonnes of cargo with a manifest showing 268 tonnes on board, and was licensed for 397 passengers with only 116 aboard; the following day he acknowledged the manifest did not accurately reflect the number of people on board.

Social activist Sherlina Nageer and a small group of women were arrested while protesting for Edghill's removal during the National Prayer Service at the Kingston Seawall Bandstand, and were subsequently released on self-bail.
The joint opposition comprising WIN, FGM, AFC, VPAC and other opposition representatives demanded Edghill's immediate resignation.
Opposition Leader Azruddin Mohamed said he believes Edghill should be held criminally responsible: 'Edghill should have been in the lockup since this incident happened.'

Dr Terrence Campbell (APNU MP) said 'accountability must go from top to bottom' and 'It cannot be that we are so dependent on the great bishop that no one else can do what he's doing right now', referring to Edghill, a bishop in the Assemblies of God.

FGM leader and MP Amanza Walton said she would have tendered her resignation, and that Ali should have immediately required the minister, the head of MARAD and the head of the Transport and Harbours Division to proceed on leave.
WIN MP Janelle Sweatnam called for Edghill's immediate resignation along with that of MARAD Director Stephen Thomas.

The Alliance For Change called for the immediate removal of Edghill and MARAD Director General Stephen Thomas, and proposed establishing a Commission of Inquiry under the Commission of Inquiry Act, Chapter 19:03.
The Amerindian Peoples Association called for Edghill's removal and asked: 'Who oversees the operations of the vessels that they do not detect what appears to be corrupt practices in overloading?'
The APA said the normalisation of corrupt practices, which Edghill described as 'mischief', has consistently contributed to the systemic failures behind the tragedy.

Comparative precedents cited: Gabon's Transport Minister Brice Paillat resigned in March 2023 a week after the Esther Miracle ferry sank (at least 21 killed, 31 missing); South Korean Prime Minister Chung Hong-won resigned after the Sewol sinking of 16 April 2014 (476 aboard, at least 187 confirmed dead); Senegal's Transport Minister Youssouf Sakho and Armed Forces Minister Youba Sambou resigned after the MS Joola capsized in September 2002 (roughly 970 of an estimated 1,034 aboard dead or missing).
